title: Learning Math Is Learning Words
author: Michael Pershan
summary: Michael Pershan uses a counting exchange with his almost-four-year-old son, one where the boy nonsensically answers 'eight' or 'fourteen' before Pershan has them recite the number sequence together, to introduce the research finding that phonological processing (the ability to represent, remember and retrieve the sounds of language) is closely tied to early computation ability. He explains that researchers measure phonological processing through tasks like rapid automatized naming (RAN), and that a 2022 meta-analysis found phonological skills predict not just word problems but pure number computation like 5+2. Pershan connects this to his son's experience directly: correctly counting on from four to five required retrieving and sequencing memorized words ('four', 'five') under real cognitive load, a language-intensive task before it was ever a mathematical one. He's careful to note the association isn't universal, plenty of children with reading struggles don't struggle with math and vice versa, but argues the broader point stands: math depends on first memorizing an arbitrary sequence of about fifteen words by heart, in order, before any of the higher-order mathematical thinking (adding, estimating, reasoning) becomes possible. He closes by rejecting the idea of a single 'math part of the brain,' arguing instead that math learning is a dance between language, experience, and number sense visible even in something as basic as counting apples.
points: Pershan connects his son's counting mistakes directly to phonological processing research, showing a live example of language ability gating early number skill.
He cites a 2022 meta-analysis finding phonological processing skills predict not just word-problem performance but pure computation, e.g., solving 5 + 2.
He explains rapid automatized naming (RAN), a task like naming randomly sequenced colors, as one of the three ways researchers measure phonological processing.

His central claim is that math depends on memorizing about fifteen words by heart, in order, before any deeper mathematical reasoning becomes possible, an 'arbitrary-ish poem at the start of mathematics.'
quotes: For over fifty years, but probably much longer, researchers have noted that students who struggle to read often also struggle with arithmetic.
That is phonological processing, our ability to represent, remember, and retrieve the sounds of language.
In a 2022 meta-anlysis the researchers found a persistent association between phonological processing skills and certain mathematical skills.
Students who struggle to do this quickly have a nontrivial chance of struggling with computation.
But look back at the conversation I had with my son: it was a language-intensive situation.
Math, the discipline of adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing, conjecturing, estimating, reasoning, solving, depends on learning about fifteen words by heart.
Learning math is a dance between language, experience, and our natural-born number sense.
